analysis.one_liner: Ends federal price supports and production limits for sugar beets and sugarcane.
analysis.headline: Despite bipartisan sponsorship from 21 senators (7 Democrats, 13 Republicans), the Senate Agriculture Committee never acted on the bill, and the sugar price support program continued.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the federal sugar program: government price support loans for sugar beet and sugarcane growers, plus the acreage allotments and marketing quotas that control who may grow and sell sugar. It would also bar the Agriculture Secretary from ever providing price support for sugar again. The program keeps domestic sugar prices above world market levels, so repealing it would tend to lower sugar prices for consumers and reduce government lending to sugar growers.
analysis.who_benefits: Households that buy sugar and sweetened foods, food and beverage manufacturers that use sugar as an ingredient, and taxpayers who back the government's sugar loans through the Commodity Credit Corporation.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sugar price support program under the Agricultural Act of 1949, through which the Commodity Credit Corporation lends to sugar beet and sugarcane growers [S2][S3].
Terminates the acreage allotments and marketing quotas that restrict who may plant and sell sugar cane and sugar beets [S2][S3].
Prohibits the Secretary of Agriculture from making any future price support available for sugar beets or sugarcane using Commodity Credit Corporation funds or any other legal authority [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors, who would lose the price floor and production rights the program provides, with no transition assistance in the bill.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes the price floor and marketing quota rights that sugar beet and cane growers rely on, which would cut farm income in sugar-producing regions [S2][S3].

The bill contains no transition aid or phase-out for growers or processing communities; after the effective date of October 1, 1996, growers would face world-market price competition immediately [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Repealing the sugar program would spread modest savings across every household that buys food, while concentrating a real loss on a few thousand sugar growers and processors who built businesses around the program. The bill's design made that adjustment abrupt: no phase-down or buyout. An honest weighing is that consumers have paid above-world prices for sugar for decades, but this bill would have imposed the correction entirely on growers at once.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never reported it, and the 104th Congress ended with no vote ever taken.

narrative.text: Senator Judd Gregg (R-NH) introduced the bill on May 23, 1995, joined by six original cosponsors: Harry Reid (D-NV), Bill Bradley (D-NJ), Dan Coats (R-IN), Jon Kyl (R-AZ), William Cohen (R-ME), and Frank Lautenberg (D-NJ) [S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on May 23, 1995 [S5].
The bill attracted 20 cosponsors, 7 Democrats and 13 Republicans, but no action followed the referral [S4][S5].
The Agriculture Committee never reported the bill, and no vote occurred before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors are better off, because they kept the price supports and production quotas the bill would have ended, while consumers continued paying the above-market prices those supports sustain.

industries.industry: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors
industries.note: The sugar program guarantees these growers above-world-market prices through Commodity Credit Corporation loans and restricts supply through acreage allotments and marketing quotas; the bill would have ended both. Growers' benefit under the program comes directly out of the prices households and food manufacturers pay for sugar.

industries.industry: Food and beverage manufacturers using sugar
industries.note: Repeal of price supports and supply controls would tend to lower the price of sugar, a major input for candy, baked goods, and beverage makers. Lower input costs would flow partly to consumers.
